title: The Volunteer Shift Nobody at the Office Knows About
script: Narrator: [reflective] Twice a week, before the sun has fully risen, I cook breakfast for a shelter that houses women who have nowhere else to go, and almost nobody at my office has the faintest idea this is how I spend those mornings.

Narrator: [thoughtful] It isn't that I've deliberately concealed it, exactly; it's more that whenever the subject drifts anywhere close, I find a way to steer the conversation elsewhere, almost instinctively.
Narrator: [honestly] Last month, a journalist who was writing a feature on community kitchens somehow tracked me down, having heard about the shift from one of the shelter's coordinators.
Narrator: [with feeling] She wanted a photograph, a short interview, my name printed beside a headline about quiet acts of kindness that go unnoticed in the city.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Part of me, I'll admit, was flattered, which surprised me more than the offer itself did, given how little I usually crave that sort of attention.
Narrator: [reflective] If the article had run, colleagues who currently assume I'm simply bad at replying to early morning messages would have finally understood where I disappear to.
Narrator: [honestly] Even so, the more I pictured my face in print, the more uneasy I became, as though something I'd been doing quietly was about to be repurposed into something performed.
Narrator: [determined] So I turned the offer down, and suggested she interview the shelter's founder instead, since the kitchen would not exist at all without her tireless effort.
Narrator: [sincere] I don't say this to suggest that nobody should ever be photographed doing good; plenty of good is done publicly for perfectly good reasons.
Narrator: [thoughtful] For me specifically, though, I've noticed that the moment an act starts feeling like it's being witnessed, some quieter, purer version of my intention starts slipping away.
Narrator: [reflective] I'd rather keep this particular habit small and unremarkable, something between myself, the tired women eating breakfast, and whoever it is I'm ultimately doing it for.
Narrator: [peacefully] So the shifts continue, unmentioned and unphotographed, and if my coworkers ever do find out, I suspect it won't be from me.

quiz.explanation: She cooks breakfast for a shelter that houses women who have nowhere else to go, before sunrise, twice a week.

quiz.explanation: She suggested interviewing the shelter's founder, since the kitchen would not exist without her tireless effort.

title: Splitting the Weeks We Never Split Evenly
script: Yoga: [tired] Siti, I need to talk about Dad's care schedule. I can't keep taking every single weekend shift.
Siti: [guarded] I did offer to help back in March, if you remember, and you told me you had it handled.
Yoga: [sighing] I know, I know. I underestimated how draining this would become, especially now that his memory is slipping too.
Siti: [carefully] Can I be honest about something that's been sitting with me for weeks?
Yoga: [wary] Go ahead.
Siti: [measured] Growing up, Dad made it fairly obvious you were the one he was proud of, and I was the one he simply tolerated.
Yoga: [defensive] That's not entirely fair, Siti.
Siti: [gently] Maybe not entirely, but it's not entirely untrue either, and I think it's part of why I've hesitated to volunteer more.
Yoga: [quiet] I never realized you carried that around all this time.
Siti: [reflective] I didn't want it to sound like an accusation. I'm telling you because I still want to help, in spite of it.
Yoga: [surprised] In spite of it? I would have understood if you'd stayed away entirely.
Siti: [thoughtful] I considered that, honestly. But whatever he did or didn't give me as a father, caring for him now isn't a debt he gets to collect or cancel.
Yoga: [moved] That's a more generous way of looking at it than I would have managed, in your position.
Siti: [sincere] It's not generosity toward him, really. It's more that I don't want to become someone who only shows up where love was shown to her first.
Yoga: [thoughtful] So where does that leave us, practically speaking?
Siti: [determined] Split the week evenly, starting this Saturday. I'll take Tuesdays and Thursdays, you keep the weekends, and we split appointments as they come up.
Yoga: [relieved] That sounds fair. More than fair, actually, given everything you've just told me.
Siti: [warmly] It's fair to him too, which matters more to me than it being fair between us.
Yoga: [quietly] Thank you, Siti. I don't think I ever properly said that.
Siti: [gently] You don't need to. Just show up on Tuesday and let me sleep in for once.

He is exhausted and their father's memory is slipping too
He no longer wants to help
He has a new job
quiz.explanation: Yoga admits he underestimated how draining it would become, especially with their father's memory now slipping.

quiz.explanation: Siti says their father made it obvious Yoga was the one he was proud of, while she was simply tolerated.

options: She wants their father's inheritance
Caring for him now isn't a debt he gets to collect or cancel

quiz.explanation: She explains that whatever their father did or didn't give her, caring for him now isn't a debt he can collect or cancel.

options: Yoga will handle everything alone

quiz.explanation: They agree to split the week evenly: Siti takes Tuesdays and Thursdays, Yoga keeps weekends, and appointments are split.

options: She wants credit for being generous
Because that priority matters more to her than fairness between herself and Yoga
She wants Yoga to feel guilty

quiz.explanation: Siti says the arrangement being fair to their father matters more to her than it being fair between the two of them.

title: The Envelope Under the Door
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] For the better part of a year, on the first of every month, I've slipped an envelope of cash under the door of the family renting the unit below mine.
Narrator: [reflective] Their situation isn't a secret exactly, everyone on the floor knows the father's been out of steady work since the factory downsized, but nobody talks about it.
Narrator: [honestly] I started small, an amount that wouldn't be missed from my budget, uncertain whether it would even help or go unnoticed among their bills.
Narrator: [thoughtful] What mattered to me was that it arrived without a name, so receiving it wouldn't cost them anything in dignity, the way a direct offer sometimes does.
Narrator: [with feeling] Last week, the wife knocked on my door holding the envelope, and I nearly panicked before realizing she wasn't accusing me of anything.
Narrator: [honestly] She'd worked out, through elimination, that my schedule was the only one matching the timing.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She didn't ask me to confirm it; she just stood there, eyes wet, saying she wanted whoever it was to know how much it had meant.
Narrator: [honestly] I could have denied it, but lying to her face felt like a smaller betrayal than being found out, and a betrayal nonetheless.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Since then, things have been slightly awkward between us, an occasional nod that carries more weight than it used to.
Narrator: [reflective] I worry that being known might change why I keep doing it, that some quiet corner of my intention could start performing for an audience of one.
Narrator: [determined] So this month, I asked her not to mention it to anyone, and I've started varying the day I leave it, hoping to blur the pattern again.
Narrator: [sincere] Whether that's overthinking a simple kindness, I couldn't say, but I'd rather guard it too carefully than let it drift into something I'm secretly proud of.
Narrator: [peacefully] The envelope still goes under the door every month, known or not, because the reason I started never depended on anyone noticing in the first place.

quiz.explanation: On the first of every month, he slips an envelope of cash under the door of the family renting the unit below his.

quiz.explanation: She worked it out through a process of elimination involving every neighbor on the floor, based on matching schedules.

quiz.explanation: Although tempted to deny it, he told her the truth because lying to her face felt like a smaller but still real betrayal.

options: He stopped giving the money entirely

quiz.explanation: He asked her not to mention it to anyone else and started varying the day, hoping to blur the pattern again.

title: The Bag Left on the Back Seat
script: Host: [warmly] My guest tonight drives for a ride-hailing app, and last month he found himself holding cash most of us would struggle to walk away from. Welcome, Pak Dedi.
Guest: [pleasantly] Thank you for having me. I still find it strange being interviewed about something so ordinary to me.
Host: [curious] Ordinary is exactly the word I want to challenge. Walk us through what happened.
Guest: [thoughtful] A passenger left a bag on the back seat after a short trip, and inside it was an envelope stuffed with cash, clearly meant for some kind of payment.
Host: [interested] Did you count it?
Guest: [honestly] Eventually, yes, once I'd pulled over somewhere safe. It came to an amount close to two months of my usual income, not a small figure for someone in my line of work.
Host: [probing] Be honest with our listeners. Did the thought of simply keeping it cross your mind, even briefly?
Guest: [candidly] Of course it did. I'd be lying if I claimed otherwise, and lying isn't something I want to model for anyone listening.
Host: [gently] What tipped the scale toward returning it?
Guest: [reflective] Two things, really. First, that money wasn't earned by me, so keeping it would mean building something on a foundation that was never mine to begin with.
Guest: [thoughtful] Second, I kept picturing whoever it belonged to, panicking, possibly owing that money to someone else, maybe someone far less forgiving than I would have been.
Host: [curious] How did you eventually get it back to them?
Guest: [warmly] The app has a system for this, thankfully. I reported it immediately, and the passenger was traced within a few hours.
Host: [interested] Was there a reward offered?
Guest: [honestly] He insisted, practically forced a portion into my hands, but I only accepted enough to cover my fuel that week and nothing more.
Host: [thoughtful] Some would call that foolish, leaving money like that on the table.
Guest: [sincere] Maybe by some counting it is. But by mine, whatever I'd have spent that money on wouldn't have brought me the same peace this decision did.
Host: [warmly] A generous way to close out our conversation. Thank you, Pak Dedi.
Guest: [warmly] Thank you for listening, and for treating an ordinary decision as though it mattered.

quiz.explanation: A passenger left a bag on the back seat containing an envelope stuffed with cash meant for some kind of payment.

quiz.explanation: He says the amount came to close to two months of his usual income.

options: The guest tracked him down himself

quiz.explanation: He reported it immediately through the app's system, and the passenger was traced within a few hours.

quiz.explanation: Although the passenger insisted, the guest only accepted a small amount, enough to cover his fuel that week.

title: The Hours Between Three and Four
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Nobody in my household knows that I wake most nights, somewhere between three and four, to pray while everyone else is still deeply asleep.
Narrator: [reflective] It began almost by accident, during a stretch of insomnia two years ago, when I decided the sleepless hours might as well be spent on something worthwhile.
Narrator: [honestly] What surprised me was how quickly it stopped feeling like a coping strategy and started feeling like the part of my day I actually looked forward to.
Narrator: [thoughtful] My sister, who shares a wall with my room, occasionally asks whether I've been sleeping poorly, having heard faint movement through the wall at strange hours.
Narrator: [honestly] I usually just say I got up for water, which isn't exactly a lie, since I do drink a glass afterward, but it isn't the whole truth either.
Narrator: [reflective] A friend at the mosque once encouraged me to mention it in our small study group, arguing that hearing about it might motivate other women to try it themselves.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I turned the idea over for days, genuinely unsure whether sharing it would inspire anyone or simply hollow something out that currently feels entirely mine.
Narrator: [with feeling] There's a particular stillness to praying while the rest of the city sleeps, unwatched, unrecorded, with no possibility of anyone's approval reaching me afterward.
Narrator: [honestly] If I described it out loud, I suspect some tiny, dishonest part of me would start waking up partly to have something to say about it later.
Narrator: [reflective] That's not a risk I'm willing to take with the one habit in my life that still feels completely uncontaminated by anyone else's opinion of me.
Narrator: [sincere] So for now, it stays quiet, between the dark room, the sound of my own voice, and whoever it is I'm actually speaking to at that hour.
Narrator: [peacefully] Some mornings I'm exhausted by breakfast, and I've stopped minding, because whatever I lose in sleep, I seem to gain back in something steadier and harder to name.

quiz.question: What does the narrator do most nights between three and four?

She checks her phone
quiz.explanation: She wakes most nights between three and four to pray while everyone else is still deeply asleep.

quiz.explanation: She feared that speaking about it might make a small, dishonest part of her start doing it partly to have something to say later.

title: Correcting the Email
script: Iqbal: [pleased] Did you see the email? The director praised the onboarding redesign in front of the whole department this morning.
Farah: [uneasy] I saw it. She mentioned my name specifically, which is the part I can't quite sit with.
Iqbal: [confused] Why not? You led the presentation.
Farah: [carefully] I presented it, yes, but the redesign itself, the actual structure, came almost entirely from Dimas's draft, back before he went on leave.
Iqbal: [dismissive] Dimas isn't even around to see the email. Nobody's going to correct the record over a wording mistake.
Farah: [firm] That's exactly what worries me. If nobody corrects it, this becomes the version of events everyone quietly accepts.
Iqbal: [reasoning] You did plenty of work refining it, though. It's not as if you're taking credit for something you never touched.
Farah: [thoughtful] I refined it, I agree, but refining someone else's foundation isn't the same as building it, and the email makes it sound like the second thing.
Iqbal: [hesitant] So what exactly are you proposing? Reply-all with a correction?
Farah: [measured] Nothing that dramatic. I'll just reply privately to the director, thank her, and mention that the core structure was Dimas's contribution before he left.
Iqbal: [skeptical] That could easily look like false modesty, you realize, especially since nobody's forcing you to say anything.
Farah: [steady] I've thought about that too, and honestly, I'd rather risk looking falsely modest than let credit settle somewhere it didn't actually belong.
Iqbal: [curious] Would you still send that message if the director never brought it up publicly at all?
Farah: [without hesitation] Yes, probably even more so, since there'd be no audience to perform the gesture in front of.
Iqbal: [reflective] I don't think I would have thought to send that message at all, if I'm being honest with myself.
Farah: [gently] Most people wouldn't, and I don't think that makes anyone dishonest, exactly, just a little less careful about where credit quietly drifts.
Iqbal: [warmly] Send it, then. And when Dimas is back, tell him yourself, before the email version becomes the only one anyone remembers.
Farah: [determined] I will. It's a small correction, but I'd rather make it now than explain it away later.

quiz.question: What did the director's email praise?
options: A marketing campaign
The onboarding redesign, mentioning Farah's name specifically
A budget proposal
A hiring decision
quiz.explanation: The director praised the onboarding redesign in front of the whole department and mentioned Farah's name specifically.

quiz.question: Why is Farah uneasy about receiving that credit?
options: She wasn't involved in the project at all
The core structure came almost entirely from Dimas's draft before he went on leave
She dislikes public praise in general
The director made a factual error about the project's timeline
quiz.explanation: Farah explains that the actual structure came almost entirely from Dimas's draft, before he went on leave.

quiz.question: What does Farah decide to do about it?
options: Reply-all to correct the record publicly
Reply privately to the director and mention Dimas's contribution
Say nothing and let it go
Ask Dimas to complain himself
quiz.explanation: She plans to reply privately to the director, thank her, and mention that the core structure was Dimas's contribution.

quiz.question: What does Iqbal warn Farah's message might look like?
options: An attempt to get promoted
False modesty
An attack on the director
A complaint about workload
quiz.explanation: Iqbal warns that her message could easily look like false modesty since nobody is forcing her to say anything.

quiz.question: Would Farah still send the message if the praise had never been public?
options: No, she would only bother if others were watching
Yes, probably even more so, since there would be no audience for the gesture
She isn't sure
She would wait for Dimas to ask her to
quiz.explanation: Farah says she would send it even more readily without an audience, since there would be nothing to perform in front of.

title: The Empty Plate on Monday
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Every Monday, I keep a voluntary fast, a habit I picked up almost two years ago after a difficult season made me want something steady to hold onto.
Narrator: [reflective] I've never announced it at work, partly because I dislike being asked questions I'd rather not turn into a whole conversation over lunch.
Narrator: [honestly] The trouble is, my team has a standing Monday tradition of ordering food together, and my empty plate has started drawing more attention than I'd like.
Narrator: [with feeling] Last week, a new colleague asked, loudly enough for half the table to hear, whether I was on some kind of diet, and something about the question made me flinch.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I could have simply said yes, diet, and let the conversation end there without any further explanation required of me.
Narrator: [honestly] Instead, almost without deciding to, I told the truth, that I was fasting, though I kept the explanation as brief as I possibly could manage.
Narrator: [reflective] Predictably, that opened a small flood of questions, why, how often, whether it was difficult, none of them unkind, but all of them more attention than I wanted.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Afterward, I found myself wishing I'd simply said nothing was wrong and let them assume I wasn't hungry that particular day.

Narrator: [honestly] What unsettled me wasn't the questions themselves, but noticing how badly I wanted the whole table to see me as disciplined, rather than simply fasting quietly like any other Monday.
Narrator: [reflective] That single flicker of wanting to be admired for it told me more about my own heart than the fast itself ever has.
Narrator: [determined] So this week, when someone glanced at my plate again, I only said I wasn't very hungry, and let the conversation move somewhere else entirely.
Narrator: [sincere] It felt like a small, almost invisible correction, choosing plainness over the version of the story that would have made me look good.
Narrator: [peacefully] The fasting itself hasn't changed at all; what changed is how carefully I'm trying to keep it between myself and the only audience that ever mattered.

quiz.question: What habit has the narrator kept for almost two years?

A voluntary fast every Monday
A weekly journal
A strict diet plan
quiz.explanation: Every Monday, he keeps a voluntary fast, a habit he picked up almost two years ago.

options: That people didn't believe him
